stem: A 70-year-old man with metastatic prostate cancer has been on a monthly depot injection of leuprolide for 3 months. Initially his bone pain worsened for a few days. He is not taking any other hormonal therapy.
oneliner: 70M + metastatic prostate cancer + monthly depot leuprolide x 3 months + initial brief flare → which hormone set now?
ask: Which set of changes best describes his hormones after 3 months?

whyNot.B: This is the **first-week flare** of an agonist (or pulsatile dosing); after months the receptors are down-regulated
whyNot.C: If LH falls, Leydig cells stop stimulation, so testosterone **cannot rise**
whyNot.D: This fits **primary testicular failure** (loss of negative feedback); his pituitary is being suppressed
whyNot.E: If LH stayed normal, Leydig cells would keep making testosterone; a lasting fall needs **less LH**, which continuous agonist exposure produces

answer: LH, FSH and testosterone all fall
why: Pulsatile GnRH stimulates the pituitary, but **continuous GnRH agonist** exposure first causes a brief **flare** and then **down-regulates GnRH receptors**. **LH and FSH fall**, so Leydig cells make less **testosterone**, giving medical castration.
chain: Pituitary GnRH receptors desensitize and down-regulate

idea.rule: Continuous GnRH shuts the axis off; pulsatile GnRH drives it.
also: Pulsatile GnRH treats hypothalamic amenorrhea or Kallmann syndrome
Leuprolide for endometriosis, fibroids, central precocious puberty
Leuprolide for estrogen-dependent breast cancer: LH and FSH fall
Continuous agonist in IVF prevents a premature LH surge

stem: A 48-year-old woman has had no menstrual periods for 4 months apart from scant spotting. She reports vaginal dryness. Her weight is stable, she does not exercise heavily, and she has no breast discharge or cold intolerance. Pregnancy test is negative.
oneliner: 48F + 4 months amenorrhea + vaginal dryness + stable weight, no galactorrhea + negative hCG → which hormone change?
ask: Which hormone change is expected?

options.D: FSH normal, LH raised, androgens raised

whyNot.B: Raised prolactin usually causes **galactorrhea**; she has **no breast discharge**
whyNot.C: Low thyroxine brings **cold intolerance**, which she **lacks**
whyNot.D: This is **PCOS**, where estrogen is preserved; her **vaginal dryness** shows low estrogen
whyNot.E: Low FSH and LH mean **hypothalamic** amenorrhea from weight loss or heavy exercise; her **weight is stable** and she does not train hard

why: With follicles running out, **estradiol and inhibin B** fall, so the pituitary is no longer restrained and **FSH** (first and most) and LH rise. Vaginal dryness reflects low estrogen.

idea.rule: Ovarian failure shows high FSH and LH with low estradiol (loss of negative feedback).
also: Primary ovarian insufficiency before age 40 gives the same pattern
Turner syndrome with streak ovaries
Hypothalamic amenorrhea: FSH and LH low
Inhibin B falls first and drives the early FSH rise

stem: Adult male rats are given an antibody that neutralizes LH. Within days, testosterone inside the testis falls sharply, yet inhibin output from the seminiferous tubules is initially unchanged. Weeks later the tubules shrink.
oneliner: Adult male rats + anti-LH antibody + intratesticular testosterone falls + inhibin unchanged at first → which cell responds to LH?
ask: Which testicular cell responds directly to LH?

whyNot.A: Sertoli cells carry **FSH receptors**; their inhibin output stayed unchanged, so they were not the LH target
whyNot.B: Germ cells **lack LH and FSH receptors**; they depend on signals from Sertoli cells and local testosterone
whyNot.D: Myoid cells **contract the tubule wall** and respond to androgen; they do not make the testosterone that fell
whyNot.E: Meiotic germ cells have **no gonadotropin receptors**; they are affected only secondarily as testosterone falls

why: **LH binds Leydig cells** in the interstitium and drives cholesterol conversion to **testosterone**. Blocking LH drops testosterone while **Sertoli function (FSH-driven)** is spared at first; tubules later shrink because spermatogenesis needs high local testosterone.
chain: Local androgen for Sertoli cells and germ cells falls
Tubules shrink; FSH rises mildly from lost feedback

idea.rule: LH acts on Leydig cells (testosterone); FSH acts on Sertoli cells (inhibin, androgen-binding protein).
also: Theca cells in the ovary are the LH target for androgens
Sertoli cells make inhibin B, which suppresses FSH
Hypogonadotropic states lower intratesticular testosterone and stop spermatogenesis

stem: A hormone is measured daily across the 28-day cycle of a healthy 25-year-old woman. Its level rises just after menses begins, dips in the middle of the follicular phase, makes a small peak at midcycle together with the LH surge, stays low through most of the luteal phase, then rises again in the last days before the next menses.
oneliner: 25F healthy + hormone curve: early follicular rise, mid-follicular dip, small midcycle peak, late luteal rise → which hormone?
ask: Which hormone does this curve show?

whyNot.B: LH makes a **tall midcycle spike**, not the small midcycle peak in the stem
whyNot.C: Estradiol **climbs steadily to a late follicular peak** and has a second luteal hump, with no late luteal rise
whyNot.D: Progesterone is **low in the follicular phase** and peaks in the mid-luteal phase, the opposite of a late luteal rise
whyNot.E: Inhibin B **peaks in the mid-follicular phase**, exactly when this hormone dips

why: **FSH rises as the corpus luteum regresses** (estradiol, progesterone and inhibin fall), recruiting the next cohort of follicles. It then **falls as estradiol and inhibin B rise**, and shows a **small surge with LH** at ovulation.
chain: Late luteal: corpus luteum fails, inhibin and steroids fall
Follicles make estradiol and inhibin B
Estradiol positive feedback gives LH surge with a small FSH peak

idea.rule: FSH is held down by estradiol and inhibin; it rises whenever those fall.
also: Menopause: low inhibin and estradiol give high FSH
Primary ovarian insufficiency: high FSH
Orchiectomy: loss of inhibin B raises FSH

stem: A healthy 27-year-old woman is on day 13 of a regular 28-day cycle. Ultrasound shows a 20 mm dominant follicle. Her estradiol has been rising for several days and is at its highest level of the cycle, while progesterone is still at follicular-phase levels. Ovulation is expected within about 36 hours.
oneliner: 27F healthy + day 13 of 28 + 20 mm follicle + estradiol at cycle peak + progesterone still low → which change triggers the LH surge?
ask: Which change triggers the LH surge?

whyNot.A: Progesterone is **still at follicular-phase levels** in the stem; its big rise comes after the surge, from the corpus luteum
whyNot.B: Inhibin B **suppresses FSH** secretion; a fall in it does not switch on LH release
whyNot.C: Prolactin **inhibits GnRH**; a rise would block ovulation in a regular cycle, not trigger it
whyNot.D: Estradiol is **at its peak in the stem**, so a fall is the wrong direction

answer: Sustained high estradiol switching to positive feedback
why: Estradiol is normally a **negative feedback** signal, but a **sustained high level** (above about 200 pg/mL for roughly 2 days) turns it into **positive feedback** on the pituitary. This produces the **LH surge** that causes ovulation.
chain: Dominant follicle makes large amounts of estradiol
High estradiol is sustained for about 2 days
Feedback switches from negative to positive
LH surge (with a small FSH surge)
Follicle ruptures about 36 hours after the surge begins

idea.rule: Sustained high estradiol is the only time estrogen gives positive feedback to the pituitary.
also: In late pregnancy estrogen is very high, but progesterone blocks a surge
Combined pills prevent the surge mainly through the progestin
Early follicular estradiol is too low and brief, so feedback stays negative

stem: Cells are isolated from an ovarian follicle and grown separately. When LH is added, one cell type makes androstenedione. These cells express LH receptors, lack aromatase, and in the intact follicle lie outside the basement membrane.
oneliner: Isolated follicle cells + LH → androstenedione, LH receptors, no aromatase, outside basement membrane → which cell?
ask: Which ovarian cell makes androstenedione under LH?

whyNot.A: Granulosa cells lie **inside the basement membrane** and have aromatase; they convert androgen to estradiol under FSH
whyNot.C: Theca externa is a **connective tissue and smooth muscle layer**, not the steroid-making layer
whyNot.D: Luteal cells appear **after ovulation**; they mainly make progesterone and are not the follicle's LH-androgen cell
whyNot.E: Surface epithelium **covers the ovary, not the follicle**, and has no steroid-making role

why: **Theca interna cells** respond to **LH** and make **androstenedione** but lack aromatase. The androgen crosses the basement membrane to **granulosa cells**, where **FSH-induced aromatase** converts it to estradiol.
chain: FSH induces aromatase in granulosa cells

idea.rule: Two-cell system: LH acts on theca (androgens); FSH acts on granulosa (aromatase and estradiol).
also: Aromatase deficiency gives high androgens and low estrogen
PCOS has excess LH-driven theca androgen
Sertoli cells in the testis also have aromatase (FSH-induced)

stem: A 29-year-old woman with infertility has regular 28-day cycles. A blood sample is drawn on day 21 to check whether she is ovulating.
oneliner: 29F + infertility + regular 28-day cycles + blood drawn day 21 → which result confirms ovulation?
ask: Which serum change on day 21 best confirms ovulation?

whyNot.A: Estradiol also rises in the **follicular phase**, so a rise does not prove the follicle ruptured
whyNot.B: FSH also falls in the **mid-follicular phase** as estradiol rises, so a low value does not prove ovulation
whyNot.C: A rise in prolactin **suppresses ovulation**; it would not confirm it in a woman with regular cycles
whyNot.E: LH is low after the surge **whether or not the follicle ruptured**, so it is not specific

why: After ovulation the **corpus luteum** secretes **progesterone**, which peaks about a week later. A **mid-luteal (day 21) progesterone** above the follicular baseline is the best serum evidence of ovulation.

idea.rule: Only a corpus luteum makes a big progesterone rise, so mid-luteal progesterone proves ovulation.
also: Basal body temperature rises after ovulation because of progesterone
Secretory endometrium on biopsy is progesterone effect
Anovulatory cycles show a low day 21 progesterone

stem: A 31-year-old woman with regular 28-day cycles has an endometrial biopsy on day 22. It shows tortuous glands with subnuclear vacuoles and an edematous stroma with early predecidual change.
oneliner: 31F + regular cycles + endometrial biopsy day 22 + tortuous glands + subnuclear vacuoles + edematous stroma → which hormone change explains this?
ask: Which hormone change explains this histology?

whyNot.A: Estradiol drives the **proliferative** phase with straight, mitotic glands, not coiled secretory glands
whyNot.B: FSH **acts on the ovary**, not directly on the endometrial glands or stroma
whyNot.D: LH acts on the ovary; it triggers ovulation but **does not act on endometrial glands**
whyNot.E: Prolactin **does not act on the endometrium** in the cycle, and a fall would not make glands secrete

answer: Increased progesterone from the corpus luteum
why: After ovulation the **corpus luteum** makes **progesterone**, which converts the endometrium to the **secretory phase**: coiled, glycogen-rich glands and edematous, predecidual stroma. This prepares the lining for implantation.

idea.rule: Straight mitotic glands = estrogen; coiled secretory glands = progesterone.
also: Progesterone withdrawal triggers menstruation
Unopposed estrogen causes endometrial hyperplasia
Anovulatory cycles stay proliferative

stem: A 28-year-old woman with regular 28-day cycles has an endometrial biopsy on day 9. It shows straight, tubular glands lined by cells with frequent mitoses. There are no secretory vacuoles.
oneliner: 28F + regular cycles + endometrial biopsy day 9 + straight glands + frequent mitoses + no secretory vacuoles → which hormone drives this phase?
ask: Which hormone drives this endometrial phase?

whyNot.B: Progesterone **produces coiled, secretory glands** after ovulation, which are not present here
whyNot.C: LH acts on the ovary and **does not stimulate endometrial growth directly**
whyNot.D: hCG is made by trophoblast **only in pregnancy**; she is cycling regularly and on day 9
whyNot.E: Prolactin acts on the **breast**, not on the proliferating endometrium

why: **Estradiol** from the growing follicle drives the **proliferative phase**: straight glands with **many mitoses** and rising progesterone-receptor expression. Before ovulation there is no progesterone effect.

idea.rule: Straight mitotic glands before ovulation = estrogen effect.
also: Unopposed estrogen causes hyperplasia
Estrogen raises its own endometrial progesterone receptors
Tamoxifen has estrogen-like action on the endometrium

stem: A 30-year-old woman is at 6 weeks' gestation by her last menstrual period. Her serum hCG is rising appropriately, and her serum progesterone is in the normal range for early pregnancy.
oneliner: 30F + 6 weeks' gestation + hCG rising + normal early-pregnancy progesterone → main progesterone source?
ask: Which structure is the main source of progesterone at this stage?

whyNot.A: Syncytiotrophoblast makes hCG now but takes over progesterone only at **about 8 to 10 weeks**, later than 6 weeks
whyNot.B: Cytotrophoblast is the **inner stem-cell layer**; placental hormones come from the syncytiotrophoblast it forms
whyNot.C: Corpus albicans is the **fibrous scar** of a regressed corpus luteum and makes no hormones
whyNot.D: Fetal adrenal supplies **DHEA-S for placental estrogen**, not progesterone

why: Until about **8 to 10 weeks**, the **corpus luteum** makes the progesterone that maintains the pregnancy. It is kept alive by **hCG** from the syncytiotrophoblast, then the **placenta** takes over (the luteal-placental shift).
chain: hCG acts on LH receptors of the corpus luteum
Placenta takes over progesterone production at 8 to 10 weeks
Corpus luteum is no longer required

idea.rule: hCG keeps the corpus luteum alive until the placenta can make its own progesterone.
also: hCG shares an alpha subunit with LH, FSH and TSH and acts on LH receptors
Removing the corpus luteum before about 8 weeks causes abortion
After about 10 weeks removal is tolerated

stem: A healthy 26-year-old woman has serum hCG measured serially through pregnancy. Early on it doubles about every 2 days. It reaches a maximum of about 100,000 mIU/mL just as the placenta takes over progesterone production from the corpus luteum, then falls to a lower plateau for the rest of pregnancy.
oneliner: 26F healthy + hCG doubles every 2 days + peaks as placenta takes over progesterone + then falls to plateau → when does hCG peak?
ask: When does hCG normally peak in pregnancy?

whyNot.A: At implantation hCG is **just becoming detectable** and still doubling, not at its maximum
whyNot.C: The stem ties the peak to the **luteal-placental shift**, which happens long before 20 weeks
whyNot.D: The stem says hCG **falls to a plateau** after its peak, so it does not peak near delivery
whyNot.E: A steady rise is excluded by the stem's **fall to a plateau**

why: hCG from the syncytiotrophoblast **doubles every 2 days** early and **peaks at 8 to 10 weeks** (about 100,000 mIU/mL), then **falls to a plateau**. A level far above this suggests a **molar pregnancy** or multiple gestation.

idea.rule: hCG peaks at the end of the first trimester, when the placenta takes over.
also: Hydatidiform mole gives very high hCG
Twin pregnancy gives higher hCG
Failing early pregnancy shows slow or falling hCG

stem: A mother brings her 9-year-old daughter to a well-child visit. Growth percentiles are normal, and she has no breast or pubic hair development yet. The mother asks which change of puberty to expect first.
oneliner: 9F + normal growth + no breast or pubic hair yet + mother asks about puberty → which change comes first?
ask: Which pubertal change typically comes first in girls?

whyNot.A: Pubic hair usually follows breast budding and reflects **adrenal androgens** (adrenarche)
whyNot.B: Menarche comes **about 2 years after** breast budding, near the end of puberty
whyNot.C: Peak height velocity occurs **around mid-puberty** after breast development begins
whyNot.E: Axillary hair comes **after** pubic hair, also driven by adrenal androgens

why: Rising **GnRH pulses** increase **LH and FSH**, so the ovary makes **estradiol**, which causes **breast budding** (thelarche) as the first sign. Pubic hair, the growth spurt and **menarche about 2 years later** follow. Onset before age 8 is precocious.
chain: Growth spurt then menarche about 2 years later

idea.rule: In girls the first step of puberty is estradiol-driven breast budding.
also: Precocious puberty is breast development before age 8
Menarche follows thelarche by about 2 years
In boys, testicular enlargement is first

stem: An 11-year-old boy attends a well-child visit. Growth is normal and he has no signs of puberty yet. His parents ask which change will mark the start of puberty.
oneliner: 11M + normal growth + no pubertal signs yet + parents ask about puberty onset → first change?
ask: Which pubertal change comes first in boys?

whyNot.B: Pubic hair comes **after** testicular growth and is driven by androgens
whyNot.C: Voice deepening is a **late** change, as the larynx enlarges under testosterone
whyNot.D: Peak height velocity occurs **late in male puberty**, unlike in girls
whyNot.E: Penile growth **follows** testicular enlargement, as testosterone rises

why: Rising **GnRH pulses** raise **FSH and LH**; growth of the seminiferous tubules makes **testicular volume exceed 4 mL**, the first sign. **LH**-driven Leydig cell **testosterone** then causes penile growth, pubic hair and the later growth spurt.
chain: Penile growth, pubic hair, growth spurt follow

idea.rule: Boys start puberty with testicular enlargement, not pubic hair.
also: Girls start with breast budding
Testis above 4 mL means puberty has begun
Peak growth is late in boys and early to middle in girls

stem: A 9-year-old girl has a few pubic hairs and early breast buds at a well-child visit. Her growth is normal. There is no other sign of virilization, and the breast buds reflect ovarian estradiol.
oneliner: 9F + few pubic hairs + early breast buds + normal growth + no virilization → which source explains the pubic hair?
ask: Which hormone source best explains the pubic hair?

options.D: Pituitary LH acting on hair follicles

whyNot.A: Estradiol drives **breast development**, not sexual hair growth
whyNot.B: Ovarian androgen excess would cause **virilization**, which is absent here
whyNot.D: LH acts on **ovarian theca cells**, not on hair follicles directly
whyNot.E: Growth hormone drives **linear growth**, which is normal here, and does not grow sexual hair

why: **Adrenarche** is a rise in **DHEA-S** from the adrenal zona reticularis, which causes **pubic and axillary hair**. It is independent of **gonadarche**, which is driven by GnRH, FSH, LH and gonadal estradiol, so the hair and breast buds have different sources.
chain: Breast buds arise separately from ovarian estradiol

idea.rule: Pubic and axillary hair come from adrenal androgens; breast and gonad growth come from the gonadal axis.
also: Premature adrenarche gives hair without other puberty signs
Congenital adrenal hyperplasia raises adrenal androgens
Complete androgen insensitivity gives breasts but no pubic hair

stem: A 22-year-old long-distance runner has had no menses for 8 months. She is thin, trains twice daily, and has pain during intercourse with poor lubrication. Pregnancy test is negative, and prolactin and TSH are normal.
oneliner: 22F + thin runner + 8 months amenorrhea + dyspareunia + hCG negative + normal prolactin and TSH → which hormone pattern?
ask: Which hormone pattern is expected?

whyNot.A: **Primary ovarian insufficiency** pattern: the ovary fails and gonadotropins climb; here the suppressed site is the **hypothalamus** of a thin athlete
whyNot.B: **PCOS** pattern (high LH:FSH ratio with normal estradiol); estrogen is not normal here, as shown by her **dry, painful vagina**
whyNot.D: High estradiol would give a **thick, lubricated vagina** and menses; she has the opposite
whyNot.E: Low gonadotropins fit, but **estradiol cannot be high** when she has **estrogen-deficiency dyspareunia**

answer: Low FSH, low LH, low estradiol (functional hypothalamic amenorrhea)
why: Low energy availability from heavy training and low weight **cuts GnRH pulse frequency**, so the pituitary releases **little FSH and LH** and follicles make **little estradiol**. Low estrogen thins the vaginal mucosa, causing **dyspareunia**.
chain: Low body weight and heavy training

idea.rule: Low GnRH drive gives low FSH, LH and estradiol together.
also: Anorexia nervosa
Severe psychological stress
Kallmann syndrome (GnRH neurons never migrate)
Hyperprolactinemia (prolactin inhibits GnRH)

stem: A 23-year-old woman at 10 weeks' gestation has a routine prenatal visit. She has no tremor, palpitations, heat intolerance or goiter. Total T4 is above the reference range, while free T4 and TSH are normal.
oneliner: 23F + 10 weeks pregnant + no hyperthyroid symptoms or goiter + total T4 high + free T4 and TSH normal → which change explains it?
ask: Which change best explains these thyroid results?

options.B: Progesterone-driven rise in thyroid hormone synthesis by the gland
options.C: Prolactin-driven displacement of T4 from its binding protein
options.D: Cortisol-driven rise in free T4 release from the thyroid
options.E: hCG stimulation of the TSH receptor with suppressed TSH

whyNot.B: Extra synthesis would raise **free T4** and suppress TSH; her free T4 and TSH are **normal**
whyNot.C: Displacing T4 would **raise free T4**; hers is normal, and prolactin does not act on binding proteins
whyNot.D: Extra free T4 release would **raise free T4** and suppress TSH; her free T4 and TSH are **normal**
whyNot.E: hCG can do this at the first-trimester peak, but then **TSH would be low** and free T4 high; her TSH is **normal**

answer: Estrogen-induced rise in hepatic thyroxine-binding globulin (TBG)
why: Rising estrogen stimulates the liver to make more **TBG**, so **total T4 rises** because more hormone is bound. **Free T4 and TSH stay normal**, so she is euthyroid and needs no treatment.
chain: More T4 is bound, total T4 rises
Free T4 is regulated back to normal by the axis

idea.rule: A change in binding protein moves total hormone, not free hormone.
also: Oral contraceptives raise TBG and total T4
Nephrotic syndrome lowers TBG and total T4
Androgens and glucocorticoids lower TBG and total T4
Total cortisol rises with estrogen via CBG

stem: A 31-year-old woman is 4 months postpartum and exclusively breastfeeds, nursing every 2 to 3 hours including at night. She has had no menses since delivery, and a pregnancy test is negative.
oneliner: 31F + 4 months postpartum + nursing every few hours + no menses + hCG negative → which hormone change explains it?
ask: Which hormone change best explains her lack of menses?

options.A: Decreased prolactin secretion from the anterior pituitary
options.B: Decreased oxytocin release from the posterior pituitary
options.C: Increased FSH secretion from the anterior pituitary
options.D: Decreased GnRH pulses from the hypothalamus
options.E: Increased progesterone secretion from the corpus luteum

whyNot.A: Frequent suckling keeps prolactin **high**, not low; that is why she still makes milk
whyNot.B: Oxytocin drives **milk let-down**, not the menstrual cycle, and suckling raises it
whyNot.C: FSH is **low** here: suppressed GnRH means the pituitary releases little FSH
whyNot.E: There is no ovulation and so **no corpus luteum**; progesterone stays low

answer: Decreased GnRH (so low FSH, LH and estrogen) from prolactin
why: Suckling keeps **prolactin high**, and prolactin **inhibits hypothalamic GnRH release**. Low GnRH means **low FSH and LH**, no follicular growth, low estrogen, and so **lactational amenorrhea**.
chain: Estrogen low, no ovulation, no menses

idea.rule: High prolactin shuts the reproductive axis at the hypothalamus.
also: Prolactinoma: amenorrhea and galactorrhea
Dopamine antagonists (antipsychotics, metoclopramide) raise prolactin
Dopamine agonists (cabergoline) restore menses in prolactinoma
Lactational amenorrhea gives temporary contraception

stem: A 27-year-old woman, 2 days after an uncomplicated vaginal delivery, notes that her breasts have become full and a little milk is leaking. Her prolactin level was high throughout the pregnancy, but she produced no milk until now.
oneliner: 27F + day 2 after vaginal delivery + breasts filling with milk + prolactin high all pregnancy but no milk before → which change starts lactation?
ask: Which hormone change allows milk production to start?

options.A: Rise in progesterone from the corpus luteum
options.B: Fall in placental estrogen and progesterone
options.C: Rise in estrogen from the ovarian follicles
options.D: Fall in prolactin from the anterior pituitary
options.E: Rise in hCG from the syncytiotrophoblast

whyNot.A: Progesterone **blocks** prolactin's effect on the breast, so a rise would keep milk away
whyNot.C: Estrogen also **blocks** the breast response to prolactin; it falls after delivery
whyNot.D: Prolactin stays **high**; its fall would stop milk, not start it
whyNot.E: hCG **falls** after the placenta is delivered, and it has no role in milk production

answer: Fall in estrogen and progesterone after delivery of the placenta
why: During pregnancy **estrogen and progesterone block** prolactin's action on the breast. Once the **placenta is delivered** they drop sharply, so the already high prolactin can act and **milk comes in** at 2 to 3 days.
chain: Block on prolactin's breast action is lifted
Milk comes in by day 2 to 3

idea.rule: Pregnancy holds prolactin's effect back; delivery of the placenta releases it.
also: Progesterone withdrawal is the main trigger for milk coming in
Retained placental fragments can delay milk coming in
Estrogen-containing contraceptives can reduce milk supply

stem: A 61-year-old man has a complete spinal cord injury at T10 from a fall. He has no sensation below the umbilicus, yet touching his penis still produces a firm erection. He asks whether sildenafil could help him.
oneliner: 61M + complete cord injury at T10 + no sensation below umbilicus + erection on touching penis + asks about sildenafil → which pathway mediates the erection?
ask: Which pathway mediates his reflex erections?

options.A: Descending fibers from the brain running through the cord
options.B: Somatic motor fibers of the pudendal nerve acting alone
options.C: Hypogastric nerve fibers mediating seminal emission
options.D: Sensory fibers of the ilioinguinal nerve to the scrotum
options.E: Parasympathetic S2–S4 via the pelvic splanchnic nerves

whyNot.A: A **complete** T10 injury cuts all descending input, yet he still gets an erection to **touch alone**
whyNot.B: The pudendal nerve carries the **sensory limb and bulbospongiosus motor** fibers; it does not dilate the arteries
whyNot.C: The hypogastric nerve is **sympathetic** and drives **emission**, not vasodilation
whyNot.D: The ilioinguinal nerve is **sensory to the groin and scrotum**; it has no erectile function

answer: Sacral parasympathetic outflow (S2–S4) releasing nitric oxide
why: The reflex arc (pudendal afferent, **sacral cord**, **pelvic splanchnic efferent**) lies **below** a T10 injury, so it survives. Its parasympathetic fibers release **nitric oxide**, raising **cGMP** in the corpora cavernosa, which is the pathway sildenafil boosts.
chain: Afferent signal via pudendal nerve to sacral cord
Reflex efferent in S2–S4 pelvic splanchnic nerves

idea.rule: Point, squeeze, shoot: parasympathetic erection, sympathetic emission, somatic ejaculation.
also: Sympathetic T11–L2 (hypogastric nerve) causes emission
Pudendal nerve (S2–S4) causes ejaculation via bulbospongiosus
Cavernous nerve injury in prostatectomy causes erectile dysfunction
PDE5 inhibitors prevent cGMP breakdown

stem: A 29-year-old woman at 24 weeks' gestation has sharp groin pain when she stands or turns over in bed, and a waddling gait. Ultrasound shows widening of the pubic symphysis.
oneliner: 29F + 24 weeks pregnant + groin pain on standing and turning + waddling gait + wide pubic symphysis → which hormone loosens the joints?
ask: Which hormone most directly loosens her pelvic ligaments?

options.C: Relaxin from the corpus luteum and placenta
options.D: Human placental lactogen from the placenta

whyNot.A: Oxytocin causes **uterine contraction and let-down**, not ligament laxity
whyNot.B: Prolactin prepares the **breast for lactation**; it does not act on pelvic joints
whyNot.D: hPL is a **diabetogenic** hormone that raises maternal glucose and insulin resistance
whyNot.E: Cortisol excess weakens **skin and bone** but is not the pregnancy hormone for pelvic ligaments

why: **Relaxin** from the corpus luteum and placenta, with **estrogen**, loosens pelvic ligaments and softens the symphysis so the birth canal can widen. The **widened symphysis** and pain on movement are the result.
chain: Corpus luteum and placenta secrete relaxin
Relaxin with estrogen softens pelvic ligaments
Pubic symphysis and sacroiliac joints loosen
Pain and waddling gait on movement

idea.rule: Pregnancy hormones prepare the pelvis and cervix for delivery.
also: Relaxin softens the cervix
Progesterone relaxes uterine smooth muscle
Estrogen raises uterine oxytocin receptors
Symphysis pubis dysfunction of pregnancy
